t.1.93.1: Śaṃtanu said: Who, then, is this one named Āpava, and what was the misdeed of the Vasus, because of whose curse they all came into a human body?
t.1.93.2: And what had been done by this boy given by Gaṅgā, on account of whose very deed he will dwell among humans?
t.1.93.3: How indeed were those Vasus, lords of the whole world, born among humans? Tell me that, O Jāhnavī.
t.1.93.4: Thus addressed, Gaṅgā, the goddess Jāhnavī, then spoke these words to the king, her husband Śaṃtanu, bull among men.
t.1.93.5: The son whom Varuṇa obtained long ago, O best of the Bhāratas, was the sage named Vasiṣṭha, who was also known as Āpava.
t.1.93.6: His hermitage was holy, thronged with flocks of beasts and birds, lying on the slope of Meru, the lord of mountains, and covered with the flowers of every season.
t.1.93.7: O best of the Bharatas, in that forest of sweet roots, fruits and water, the son of Varuṇa, foremost among the doers of merit, practiced austerities.
t.1.93.9: For the benefit of the world, that righteous-souled son of Varuṇa obtained that excellent cow, the yielder of all desires, as his oblation-cow.
t.1.93.8: That daughter of Dakṣa who was highly renowned as Surabhī, that goddess bore a cow by Kaśyapa, O bull among the Bharatas.
t.1.93.10: Then that cow, dwelling in that forest of ascetics frequented by sages, delightful and righteous, roamed about free from fear.
t.1.93.11: Then once, O bull among the Bharatas, all the Vasus, led by Pṛthu, came to that forest frequented by gods and divine seers.
t.1.93.12: Together with their wives, they wandered all over that forest, and they took their pleasure on the delightful mountains and in the lovely woods.
t.1.93.13: There, O you whose valor equals Vāsava's, the slender-waisted wife of one of the Vasus, wandering in that forest, saw a cow, the one belonging to the sage Vasiṣṭha, the finest of cows, yielding every desire.
t.1.93.14: Filled with wonder at the cow's wealth of fine qualities, she showed that cow to Dyu, O bull-eyed one.
t.1.93.16: Long ago, O lord of kings, O joy of the Pauravas, the Vasu's beloved wife showed that cow, endowed with such virtues, to the Vasu.
t.1.93.15: Cherished by good friends, she was an excellent milker, auspicious, with a lovely tail and face, endowed with every good quality and with an unsurpassed gentle nature.
t.1.93.18: This excellent cow, O goddess with dark eyes, belongs to Vāruṇi, O lady of fair hips, that seer to whom this excellent forest belongs.
t.1.93.17: Then Dyaus, as soon as he saw that cow, O king whose valor rivals that of Indra and the lord of elephants, spoke to that goddess, his wife, describing the cow's beauty and fine qualities.
t.1.93.19: O slender-waisted one, the mortal who drinks the sweet milk of this cow would live for ten thousand years with his youth unfading.
t.1.93.20: Having heard this, O best of kings, that goddess of slender waist and faultless limbs spoke to her husband of blazing splendor.
t.1.93.21: In the world of men I have a friend, the daughter of a king, Jinavatī by name, endowed with beauty and youth.
t.1.93.22: The daughter of Uśīnara, the wise royal sage true to his vow, was renowned in the world of men for the splendor of her beauty.
t.1.93.23: For her sake, O fortunate one, bring me the cow with her calf that I desire; bring her quickly, O best of the immortals, O increaser of merit.
t.1.93.24: So that, having drunk her milk, that friend of mine, O giver of honor, may become the one person among humans free from old age and disease.
t.1.93.26: Having heard these words of the goddess, Dyu, wishing to do what was dear to her, then carried off that cow together with his brothers, Pṛthu and the others.
t.1.93.25: O greatly fortunate one, O blameless one, you ought to do this kindness for me, for there is nothing else whatsoever dearer to me than this.
t.1.93.28: Then Vāruṇi, having gathered fruits, reached his hermitage, but he did not see the cow with her calf there in that finest of forests.
t.1.93.27: Urged then by that lotus-petal-eyed woman, O king, Dyaus could not see the fierce austerity of that seer. The cow was then carried off by him, but the fall that would follow was not foreseen.
t.1.93.29: Then that ascetic, rich in austerities, searched for her in that forest, but the noble-minded sage, though searching, did not find that cow.
t.1.93.30: Knowing through his divine sight that she had thus been carried off by the Vasus, he at once fell under the sway of anger and then cursed the Vasus.
t.1.93.31: Because the Vasus carried off my milk-giving cow with the beautiful tail, therefore they shall all be born among men; of this there is no doubt.
t.1.93.32: Thus, O bull of the Bharatas, did the blessed Āpava, best of sages, having fallen under the sway of anger, curse those Vasus.
t.1.93.33: Having cursed them, the illustrious one set his mind on austerity alone. Thus, O king, did that sage rich in austerity, the brahmarṣi of great power, filled with wrath, curse the eight Vasus, the gods.
t.1.93.35: Though the Vasus sought to appease that seer, O bull among kings, they did not obtain his grace, O tiger among men, from Āpava, that best of seers, learned in every dharma.
t.1.93.34: Then, having come once more to the hermitage of that great-souled one, and knowing, “We have been cursed,” they approached the seer.
t.1.93.36: And that righteous-souled one said: "You seven, Dhara and the others, shall indeed obtain release from the curse after a year."
t.1.93.37: But this Dyau, on whose account you were all cursed by me, will then dwell in the world of men for a long time because of his own deed.
t.1.93.39: He will be righteous in spirit, skilled in all the śāstras, devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial to his father, and he will renounce the pleasures of women. Having spoken thus to all the Vasus, the blessed seer departed.
t.1.93.38: I do not wish to make false what I said to you in anger. And this great-minded one shall not beget offspring among men.
t.1.93.40: Then all the Vasus came to me and asked a boon of me, O king, and I granted it: "As soon as each of us is born, O Gaṅgā, cast us yourself into the water."
t.1.93.41: Thus, O best of kings, I have duly acted for those who were cursed, so that they might be properly released from the world of men.
t.1.93.43: Having told this, the goddess vanished right there; and taking that boy with her, she then went wherever she wished.
t.1.93.42: Because of that ṛṣi's curse, O best of kings, this one alone, Dyau, will dwell for a long time in the world of men, O king, O Bhārata.
t.1.93.44: He was named Devavrata and was also called Gāṅgeya; thus the son of Śaṃtanu bore two names, and he surpassed Śaṃtanu in virtues.
t.1.93.45: And Śaṃtanu too, stricken with grief, then went to his own city. I shall now recount the boundless virtues of that Śaṃtanu.
t.1.93.46: And I shall also tell of the great fortune of the illustrious king Bhārata, whose splendid history is called the Mahābhārata.
